items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And I also did an album with Basie for Kay Starr

ctx.x: When you wrote for the Basie band, were there particular soloists at that time that you kept in mind?

Well the things I did for Basie, if I can remember, were as it happened, I think Teddy Reig had a notion that I could write for singers with the Basie band. I think the first thing I did was something or other for a television show, and I don’t remember who the singer was, and on the strength of that I began to do other things for the Basie band in a similar way. I did an album for Arthur Prysock and I remember that Prysock’s key turned out to be E major, an unusual one.

items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: If it was a swing kind of thing you’d put in Count Basie things here and there.

ctx.x: The typical part you’d get on a pop session, did it have chord symbols and just an indication of what to do?

Yeah. Even, this is the strange thing, that in most situations even if the rest of the band was highly organized, the piano part was really almost always an automatic copying job in which you really reading the bass part and the guitar part and being encouraged to do what was necessary. The piano player would figure out what I call the in-betweens. If it was a swing kind of thing you’d put in Count Basie things here and there. And in other cases it might be that you should be playing in two or playing in four,…

part exactly the way it was with no fill-ins, and sometimes there are some wide open opportunities to do something that the arranger hadn’t thought of. And if you were diplomatic about it he might appreciate very much if you gave a slightly different cast to what he wanted.
